title: Sliding Doors
events_chronological: Helen Quilley is sacked from her London PR job and heads home in the middle of the morning.
She runs down the steps to the Underground, and the story splits at the closing doors of the train.
In the first branch she catches the train, meets James, and gets home to find her boyfriend Gerry in bed with his ex, Lydia.
She leaves Gerry the same day and moves in with her friend Anna.
She cuts and dyes her hair and starts a PR agency of her own with James egging her on.
In the second branch she misses the train, is mugged on the way out, and reaches the flat after Lydia has gone.
She takes two jobs, delivering sandwiches and pulling pints, to keep Gerry writing his unwritten novel.
Gerry keeps seeing Lydia and keeps lying about it, and Lydia starts pressing him to choose.
In the first branch Helen and James fall in love, and Helen learns she is pregnant.
Helen sees James with another woman, assumes he is married, and walks out on him.
In the second branch Helen finds she is pregnant by Gerry and plans to tell him over dinner.
Lydia turns up at the same restaurant and tells Gerry that she is pregnant too.
In the first branch James finds Helen and explains that the woman is his wife, whom he is divorcing.
Helen steps into the road and is hit by a car, and both branches converge on the same hospital.
In the first branch Helen loses the baby and dies with James beside her.
In the second branch Helen loses the baby but survives, and finally throws Gerry out.
Leaving the hospital in a lift, Helen drops an earring and a stranger picks it up: James.
syuzhet_notes: The film splits at told-order bullet 2 and then runs two mutually exclusive versions of the same months side by side, cutting between them every few minutes and using Helen's haircut to keep them apart. Because the branches are simultaneous rather than sequential, nearly every jump in told order is lateral - into the other timeline at roughly the same date - rather than forward or backward.
fabula_notes: The two branches cannot both be true, so this chronology lays them out as parallel tracks ordered by date rather than as a single causal sequence. The closing scene implies that the surviving Helen carries something over from the branch that ended, which no ordering can represent.
